title: Lemon and ginger fudge
subtitle: creamy vanilla fudge with sharp lemon and warm ground ginger
excerpt: Lemon and ginger fudge uses condensed milk as the base, which makes a reliably smooth, creamy result without a sugar thermometer, provided you watch the pan carefully and test a small amount in cold water. The lemon zest is added off the heat so the flavour stays bright. Ground ginger gives warmth without overpowering the citrus.
sourceNotes: Condensed milk fudge method documented in British cookery books from the mid-twentieth century onward. Lemon and ginger flavouring combination from British confectionery tradition.

glossaryTerms.definition: A sugar cooking stage reached at 112 to 116°C. A small amount of syrup dropped into cold water forms a soft, pliable ball that flattens when pressed. Used for fudge, fondant, and Italian meringue.

recipe.freezeNotes: Wrap individual pieces in waxed paper and freeze in an airtight container for up to 3 months. Thaw at room temperature for 30 minutes.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keeps in an airtight tin at room temperature for up to 2 weeks.
recipe.temperatureNote: soft ball stage (116°C on a sugar thermometer, or forms a soft ball in cold water)

content.text: at about 116°C. If you do not have a sugar thermometer, test by dropping a small amount of the boiling mixture into a glass of very cold water: when it forms a soft, pliable ball that flattens between your fingers, it is ready. The key difference from toffee is that the temperature is lower and you beat the mixture vigorously once off the heat, which creates the fine-grained, creamy texture.
Grease and line a 20 cm square tin with baking parchment.

Put the sugar, butter, condensed milk, and whole milk into a medium heavy-based saucepan. Heat over a low heat, stirring constantly, until the sugar has dissolved and the butter has melted. Do not let it boil before the sugar is fully dissolved.

Increase the heat to medium and bring to a steady boil, stirring continuously. The mixture will spit. Cook for about 15 to 20 minutes, stirring constantly, until it reaches 116°C or passes the cold water test. The mixture will have darkened slightly and thickened.
Remove from the heat and stir in the lemon zest, lemon juice, and ground ginger immediately.
Beat vigorously with a wooden spoon or silicone spatula for about 5 minutes until the fudge thickens, loses its gloss, and starts to look grainy and dull. This is the correct texture.
Pour into the prepared tin and smooth the surface. Leave to cool at room temperature for 2 hours until set. Score into squares with a sharp knife. Turn out and cut along the score lines.

attrs.problem: Fudge is very soft and does not set
attrs.avoid: Avoid removing from the heat before the soft ball stage is reached.
attrs.fix: Return the fudge to the saucepan with a splash of milk, re-heat, and cook on to the correct temperature before beating again.

attrs.problem: Fudge is very grainy and crumbly
attrs.avoid: Avoid over-beating; stop as soon as the fudge loses its gloss and thickens.
attrs.fix: If already in the tin, the texture will not change, but the flavour is the same. Serve as crumbled pieces over ice cream rather than neat squares.
